reasoning: The pool reframes the item away from the clinical diagnosis I generated in Stage 1 (hypertensive urgency) toward the underlying system/management problem, and the condition pool contains no clinical option at all — C1, C2, and C3 are all communication or competence framings. Within that pool, C1 is the only option the stem supports: the stem states explicitly that the 1800 monitoring check was missed 'after an incomplete, dismissive handoff,' which links a communication failure directly to a care omission with client-safety consequences (an unmonitored 186/102 with headache after a same-day amlodipine increase). C2 is contradicted because an omitted ordered assessment is by definition more than friction requiring no intervention. C3 is contradicted because the stem attributes the failure to the handoff given to Priya, not to Priya's knowledge; Priya in fact correctly recognized and escalated the abnormal BP. For actions, client safety precedes personnel management: A1 operationalizes the standing order (call if SBP > 180, and 186 breaches it) and includes the missed monitoring intervals, which the provider needs to interpret the value. A2 is the correct second action because addressing the handoff failure requires a private, behavior-specific, policy-based conversation with the responsible staff member, including documentation. A3 is contradicted because it inverts the priority, delaying provider notification for an interpersonal issue. A4 is contradicted because absence of harm does not remove the obligation to document a care omission and notify the manager per policy; near misses are reportable. For parameters, the evaluation must match the selected condition rather than the clinical picture: P2 measures whether the handoff process itself improved (completeness, professionalism, medication changes communicated, time for questions), and P3 measures the downstream client-safety outcome (q4h monitoring actually performed, no further omissions). P1 is a clinical parameter with no stem basis — no labs, renal history, or end-organ findings are given — and it evaluates Mrs. Vega's kidneys rather than the communication breakdown. P4 measures a social outcome that is not a professional-practice endpoint and would be inappropriate as a resolution criterion.
